content.text: Chapter Three, “Current Electricity,” studies charges in motion and the basic laws governing steady electric currents. Earlier electrostatics considered charges at rest. Lightning is an example of a non-steady flow of charge, whereas a torch and a cell-driven clock illustrate devices with more steady currents.

Consider an area normal to charge flow. Let q+ be the net positive charge moving forward and q− the net negative charge moving forward during time t. The net forward charge is q = q+ − q−. For steady current, this charge is proportional to time, and current is charge transported per unit time. A negative value indicates current in the backward direction. The SI unit is ampere (A).

For a time-varying current, let ΔQ be the net charge crossing a conductor cross-section between t and t + Δt. The instantaneous current is the limit of ΔQ/Δt as Δt tends to zero. The chapter notes that domestic-appliance currents are typically of order amperes, lightning currents can be tens of thousands of amperes, and currents in nerves are in microamperes.

A charge experiences force in an electric field and contributes to current if it is free to move. In metals, some electrons are practically free within the material; in solid conductors the current is carried by negatively charged electrons against a background of fixed positive ions. Electrolytic solutions can carry current through both positive and negative mobile charges. Without an applied field, electron thermal velocities have random directions and average to zero, so there is no net current.

A field applied across a conductor accelerates electrons toward the positively charged end. If end charges are not replenished, electrons neutralise them and the current lasts only briefly. A steady current requires a mechanism such as a cell or battery to continually maintain the electric field.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: How a steady current is maintained

content.text: For an ohmic conductor, the potential difference V across its ends is proportional to current I: V = RI. The proportionality constant R is resistance, measured in ohms (Ω), with 1 Ω = 1 V/A. Resistance depends on both material and dimensions. Ohm’s law was discovered by G. S. Ohm in 1828.

For a slab-like conductor, doubling its length while keeping area and material unchanged doubles resistance. Cutting it lengthwise to halve its cross-sectional area doubles resistance. Thus resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. The proportionality constant is resistivity ρ, a property of the material at specified conditions.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Resistance dependence on length and area

content.text: Resistivity ρ relates resistance to geometry. For a uniform conductor of length l, the voltage drop is V = El. Current density j is current per unit area normal to flow, with SI unit A m⁻². Combining Ohm’s law with the geometric relation gives E = ρj; conductivity σ is the reciprocal of resistivity and j = σE. In vector form, current density and electric field are parallel for an ohmic isotropic conductor.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Resistivity, current density and microscopic Ohm's law

content.text: In the absence of an electric field, electron velocities after collisions are random and their average is zero. In an applied field, an electron of charge −e and mass m has acceleration a = −eE/m. If ti is the time since its last collision, its velocity is its post-collision velocity plus the acceleration term. Averaging over electrons, the random term vanishes and the mean drift velocity is opposite to E.

Let n be the number of free electrons per unit volume, A the cross-sectional area and |vd| the drift-speed magnitude. In time Δt, electrons in a length |vd|Δt cross the area. The magnitude of current is I = neA|vd|, and current density magnitude is j = ne|vd|. Using the drift-speed expression gives conductivity σ = ne²τ/m. This microscopic model reproduces Ohm’s law under the assumptions that n and average collision time τ are constants independent of E.

Problem: Estimate the average drift speed of conduction electrons in a copper wire of cross-sectional area 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ m² carrying 1.5 A, assuming one conduction electron per copper atom. Copper density is 9.0 × 10³ kg m⁻³ and atomic mass 63.5 u. The electron number density is estimated from the number of atoms per cubic metre: n = (6.0 × 10²³/63.5) × 9.0 × 10⁶ = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. With e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, vd = I/(neA) = 1.1 × 10⁻³ m s⁻¹ = 1.1 mm s⁻¹. The text compares this with copper-atom thermal speeds of about 2 × 10² m s⁻¹ at 300 K and an electric-field propagation speed of 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; drift is much slower.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Worked Example 3.1: drift speed in copper

content.text: The example asks why current is established almost instantly despite drift speeds of only a few mm/s; why electrons attain steady average drift speed despite acceleration; how a small electron charge and slow drift can produce large currents; whether all free electrons move in the same direction; and whether electron paths between collisions are straight. The supplied explanations are: the electric field is established throughout the circuit almost at light speed; electrons accelerate between collisions and lose drift speed in collisions; electron number density is enormous (~10²⁹ m⁻³); drift is superposed on random velocities; and paths are straight without a field but generally curved with a field.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Worked Example 3.2: conceptual questions on drift

content.text: Mobility μ is the magnitude of drift velocity per unit electric-field magnitude. Its SI unit is m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹. For the electron drift model, μ = eτ/m and is positive; τ is the average time between successive collisions.

Not all circuit materials and devices have a linear, unique V–I relation. Deviations include: V is not proportional to I; reversing V does not yield an equal and opposite current (as in a diode); or more than one voltage corresponds to the same current (the text gives GaAs as an example). Such non-ohmic materials and devices are widely used in electronics.

Materials are classified by increasing resistivity as conductors, semiconductors and insulators. Metals have low resistivity, roughly 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ Ω m. Insulators such as ceramics, rubber and plastics can have resistivities around 10¹⁸ times greater than metals or more. Semiconductors lie between these classes; their resistivity typically decreases with temperature and can be lowered by adding suitable impurities.

Over a limited temperature interval, a metallic conductor’s resistivity is approximately ρT = ρ0[1 + α(T − T0)], where ρ0 is resistivity at reference temperature T0 and α is the temperature coefficient of resistivity, with dimension temperature⁻¹. For metals α is positive. The relation is approximately linear only over a limited range. Nichrome, manganin and constantan have weak temperature dependence and are used in standard wire-wound resistors.

From the conduction model, ρ = m/(ne²τ), so resistivity varies inversely with carrier number density n and average collision time τ. In metals, n changes little with temperature while τ decreases as collisions become more frequent, so resistivity increases. In semiconductors and insulators, carrier density increases with temperature enough to dominate the reduction in τ, so resistivity decreases.

Problem: A toaster element has resistance 75.3 Ω at 27.0 °C and draws 2.68 A from a 230 V supply at steady state. The average temperature coefficient is 1.70 × 10⁻⁴ °C⁻¹. First calculate R2 = V/I = 230/2.68 = 85.8 Ω. Then use R2 = R1[1 + α(T2 − T1)] to obtain T2 − T1 = (85.8 − 75.3)/(75.3 × 1.70 × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 820 °C, hence T2 ≈ 847 °C. The steady state occurs when electrical heating balances heat loss.

Problem: A platinum wire has resistance 5.00 Ω at the ice point and 5.23 Ω at the steam point. In a hot bath its resistance is 5.795 Ω. Using the linear calibration relation, t = [(Rt − R0)/(R100 − R0)] × 100, the temperature is [(5.795 − 5.00)/(5.23 − 5.00)] × 100 = 345.65 °C.

For current I flowing from higher potential A to lower potential B, V = V(A) − V(B) > 0. In time Δt, charge ΔQ = IΔt moves and its electrical potential energy decreases by ΔUpot = −IVΔt. In a real conductor, collisions transfer the gained energy to atoms, heating the conductor. The energy dissipated as heat is ΔW = IVΔt.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Electrical energy dissipated in a conductor

content.text: Power dissipated is energy per unit time, P = IV. Using V = IR gives P = I²R = V²/R. This power heats resistors and can produce light, as in an incandescent bulb. The cell’s chemical energy supplies the energy in a simple cell-resistor circuit.

For a device requiring power P delivered at voltage V and current I, P = VI. If transmission cables have resistance Rc, their wasted power is Pc = I²Rc = P²Rc/V². For fixed delivered power and cable resistance, increasing transmission voltage reduces cable loss. High-voltage transmission is used over long distances, and transformers lower voltage to safer values for end use.

A cell has positive and negative electrodes immersed in an electrolyte. The electrode-electrolyte interfaces develop potential differences V+ and −V−, so the emf is ε = V+ + V− > 0. Despite its name, electromotive force is a potential difference, not a force. In an open circuit no current flows and the terminal potential difference equals the emf.

The electrolyte has finite internal resistance r. When external resistance R is connected, current I flows and the terminal voltage is V = ε − Ir. Across the external resistor, V = IR, giving I = ε/(R + r). The maximum theoretical current occurs at R = 0 and equals ε/r, although practical cells may allow a smaller maximum to avoid damage. Internal resistance may be neglected when ε ≫ Ir.

For two cells in series with emfs ε1, ε2 and internal resistances r1, r2, the equivalent emf and internal resistance are εeq = ε1 + ε2 and req = r1 + r2 when their emfs aid the current direction. If one cell is reversed, its emf enters with a negative sign; for the described opposing arrangement εeq = ε1 − ε2 (ε1 > ε2). For n cells, add internal resistances and add emfs algebraically according to orientation.

For two parallel cells with emfs ε1, ε2 and internal resistances r1, r2, the equivalent internal resistance satisfies 1/req = 1/r1 + 1/r2, while εeq/req = ε1/r1 + ε2/r2. Thus εeq = (ε1r2 + ε2r1)/(r1 + r2) and req = r1r2/(r1 + r2). For n cells, the reciprocal internal resistances add and εeq/req equals the sum of εi/ri. If one cell is oppositely oriented, its emf is assigned a negative sign.

Assign a direction to each unknown branch current. A positive solution means the current flows as assumed; a negative result means it flows opposite to the arrow. For a cell with current flowing through it from negative to positive terminal, terminal potential difference is V = ε − Ir; if the labelled current runs from positive to negative through the cell, V = ε + Ir.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Kirchhoff's rules: setup and sign conventions

content.text: At any junction, the sum of currents entering equals the sum leaving. This follows from conservation of charge: in steady state there is no accumulation of charge at a junction or point on a wire. The rule applies even when a wire bends or is reoriented.

The algebraic sum of potential changes around any closed loop is zero. Electric potential depends on position, so returning to the starting point gives zero net potential change. Apply voltage rises and drops with consistent signs.

Problem: A 10 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected across diagonally opposite corners of a cube with 12 equal resistors, each of resistance 1 Ω. By symmetry, the three edges meeting at one terminal carry equal current I, and the current splits equally at symmetric corners. Applying the loop rule to the stated loop gives −IR − (1/2)IR − IR + ε = 0, so ε = (5/2)IR. The equivalent resistance is Req = ε/(3I) = (5/6)R. For R = 1 Ω, Req = 5/6 Ω; total current is 10/(5/6) = 12 A, so I = 4 A. Individual edge currents follow from the symmetry and current splitting.

The example assigns unknown currents I1, I2 and I3 to a network and uses Kirchhoff’s junction rule to express other branch currents. Applying the loop rule to three independent loops gives: 7I1 − 6I2 − 2I3 = 10; I1 + 6I2 + 2I3 = 10; and 2I1 − 4I2 − 4I3 = −5. The printed solution reports I1 = 2.5 A, I2 = 5/8 A, and I3 = 1 7/8 A. Branch currents reported are AB = 5/8 A, CA = 2 A, DEB = 1 7/8 A, AD = 1 7/8 A, CD = 0 A, and BC = 2 1/2 A. The text verifies that the resulting currents satisfy the loop rule for other loops as well.

content.text: A Wheatstone bridge has four resistors R1, R2, R3 and R4; a source is connected across one diagonal (battery arm), and a galvanometer across the other (galvanometer arm). For a balanced bridge, galvanometer current Ig = 0. Junction and loop rules give I1 = I3, I2 = I4 and the balance condition R2/R1 = R4/R3, equivalently R1R4 = R2R3. If R4 is unknown, adjust R3 until the galvanometer shows null deflection, then R4 = R3 R2/R1. The text identifies the meter bridge as a practical device based on this principle.

Problem: Wheatstone bridge arms AB = 100 Ω, BC = 10 Ω, CD = 5 Ω, DA = 60 Ω; a 15 Ω galvanometer is connected across BD and 10 V is maintained across AC. The printed mesh equations are 20I1 + 3Ig − 12I2 = 0; 2I1 − 6Ig − I2 = 0; and 13I2 + Ig = 2. Combining the second equation multiplied by 10 with the first gives I2 = 31.5Ig. Substitution into the third yields 410.5Ig = 2 and Ig = 4.87 mA.

The chapter summary defines current as net charge passing per unit time and notes that steady current requires a closed circuit and a source that moves charge from lower to higher potential energy. Emf is work done per unit charge by the source and is the open-circuit terminal voltage, not a force. Ohm’s law is V = RI for ohmic substances; resistance is measured in ohms.

metadata.topic: Chapter summary: current, emf and Ohm's law

content.text: Resistance is R = ρl/A, where resistivity depends on material and temperature/pressure. Metals have low resistivity (about 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ Ω m); insulators may be 10²²–10²⁴ times more resistive than metals according to the summary; semiconductors lie between them on a logarithmic scale. Most current carriers are electrons, but ionic crystals and electrolytic liquids can conduct through positive and negative ions.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Chapter summary: resistivity and current carriers

content.text: The summary gives current density as j = nqvd, where n is carrier number density, q the charge per carrier and vd drift velocity. For electrons q = −e. For uniform current density normal to area A, current magnitude is ne|vd|A. The microscopic drift model gives vd = eEτ/m in magnitude and ρ = m/(ne²τ).

metadata.topic: Chapter summary: current density and microscopic model

content.text: Ohm’s law is not a fundamental law and fails for nonlinear V–I relations, polarity-dependent V–I behaviour, or non-unique voltage for a current. The summary defines the temperature coefficient α as fractional increase in resistivity per unit temperature increase over a range where resistivity increases linearly. The terminal voltage across external resistance R is Vext = IR = εR/(R + r).

content.text: The textbook includes a reference table of physical quantities and units: current I in amperes (SI base unit); charge Q in coulombs; voltage and emf in volts; resistance in ohms; resistivity in Ω m; conductivity in siemens (S); electric field in V m⁻¹; drift speed in m s⁻¹; relaxation time in seconds; current density in A m⁻²; and mobility in m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹. The extracted table’s dimension formatting is difficult to preserve perfectly, so the units and relationships are recorded here rather than guessing ambiguous exponents.

Current is a scalar even though an arrow is often drawn to indicate its direction; currents do not obey vector addition. Current through an area is the scalar product of current-density vector j and area vector ΔS.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Points to Ponder: current as a scalar

content.text: The equation V = IR can define resistance for any conducting device and by itself does not prove that the device obeys Ohm’s law. Ohm’s law means the I–V plot is linear and R is independent of V. In material form, E = ρj is Ohm’s law when resistivity does not depend on magnitude or direction of the applied electric field. Real materials obey it only within ranges of field; sufficiently strong fields cause departures.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Points to Ponder: meaning of Ohm's law

content.text: Electron motion in an electric field combines random collision-driven motion with field-induced drift; the random motion averages to zero and does not contribute to drift velocity. The relation j = ρv must be applied separately to each carrier type. In a neutral conducting wire, positive and negative charge densities cancel; because positive ions are nearly stationary, total current density is not obtained by simply multiplying total charge density by a single velocity.

The textbook identifies Georg Simon Ohm (1787–1854) as a German physicist and professor at Munich. It says he developed his law in 1828 and was guided by an analogy between heat conduction and electrical conduction: electric field corresponds to temperature gradient, and electric current corresponds to heat flow.

The textbook identifies Gustav Robert Kirchhoff (1824–1887) as a German physicist who was a professor at Heidelberg and Berlin. It notes his work on spectroscopy and his important contributions to mathematical physics, including the first and second circuit rules.
